templates.name: Period between independent clauses (second often opens with an introductory phrase)
Conjunctive adverb: semicolon or period on the correct side, comma on the other
Colon after a complete clause before an explanation or specified item
No punctuation with a restrictive clause or restrictive appositive
Dash pair around a supplementary element
Comma before a trailing nonrestrictive modifier
No punctuation between subject and verb
Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
Comma or parenthesis pair around a supplementary element
No punctuation between a verb or preposition and its object
Question versus statement (word order and end mark)
Items in a series (commas; semicolons when items contain commas)

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a gerund subject
items.passage: For centuries, European scribes wrote with iron gall ink, a mixture of crushed oak galls and iron salts that can gradually eat through the ______ affected manuscripts with calcium phytate, a compound that binds the free iron responsible for this deterioration, is now a standard conservation practice.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “For centuries, European scribes ... can gradually eat through the paper” is a complete sentence. The next sentence has its own subject, the gerund phrase “Treating affected manuscripts with calcium phytate,” and its own verb, “is,” so a period is needed between them.

A.why_wrong: Without a comma before it, “and” cannot join the two independent clauses; it also makes “treating affected manuscripts” look like a second thing the ink eats through, leaving “is” without a subject.

B.recipe: comma splice (gerund subject read as a modifier)
B.why_wrong: With a comma, “treating affected manuscripts ...” looks like a phrase describing the first clause, but it is the subject of “is,” so two independent clauses are joined by only a comma.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “paper treating affected manuscripts” runs the two sentences together.

items.notes: Subject: science and technology (manuscript conservation chemistry). Band 6: one 45-word run; the second sentence opens with a 16-word gerund subject containing an appositive, so the comma version reads at first as a participle on clause 1 (73a6603c move). Review: the “; by treating” decoy and the “slows the damage” tail made the option set and frame a mark-for-mark copy of 73a6603c; now “and treating” (1b97cce9 recipe) and a different predicate.

fixes: the “; by treating” decoy and the tail “considerably slows the damage” made the option set and frame a mark-for-mark copy of 73a6603c (“; by adding”, “helps combat this effect”): A is now “paper and treating” (conjunction without comma, as 1b97cce9) and the predicate “is now a standard conservation practice”; explanation, A and B why_wrong and notes updated
review.notes: No fact check (Boundaries, brief of 2026-10-16); named people are real and only their own known work is attributed to them; no invented names.

band7.why: Gerund-subject opener (16 words with an inner appositive) after a period key, the band-6 opener type; the comma version reads as a participle on clause 1 and the splice shows 16 words later, but no distractor is decided by meaning.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a long “Like” opener
items.passage: In the 1830s, Finnish physician Elias Lönnrot traveled through Karelia transcribing folk songs, then wove them into a single ______ the Homeric epics, which grew out of centuries of oral performance, the resulting Kalevala has roots in a collective tradition.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “a single poem.” The phrase “Like the Homeric epics, which grew out of centuries of oral performance” describes the subject of the next sentence, “the resulting Kalevala,” which has its own verb, “has.” A period is needed between the two sentences.

B.recipe: comma splice (opener read as a modifier of clause 1)
B.why_wrong: The comma makes “like the Homeric epics ...” seem to describe “poem,” but “the resulting Kalevala has roots ...” is a second independent clause, so the two clauses are joined with only a comma.

C.why_wrong: Without punctuation, “poem like the Homeric epics” attaches the phrase to the first clause, and the comma before “the resulting Kalevala” then splices two independent clauses.

D.why_wrong: “That” begins a clause that never gets a verb of its own, because “the resulting Kalevala has roots ...” supplies a new subject; the sentence breaks.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Finnish epic). Band 7: an 11-word “Like” opener with its own which-clause that reads as a modifier of clause 1’s last noun until “the resulting Kalevala has” arrives 11 words after the blank; run of 40 words. Opener type not used in b1 to b3.

review.notes: No fact check (Boundaries, brief of 2026-10-16); named people are real and only their own known work is attributed to them; no invented names.

band7.why: 11-word “Like” opener with its own which-clause attaches naturally to clause 1’s last noun (“a single poem like the Homeric epics”); the splice shows only at “the resulting Kalevala has,” 11 words past the blank; 40-word run; distractors are the band-7 S1_period set (splice, glued, “that,” added word).

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing clause 1, semicolon before an explanation
items.passage: Leaves make an unpromising diet for most birds: they are bulky, nutritionally poor, and difficult to digest. The hoatzin of South American wetlands is remarkably well equipped for such a ______ its enlarged crop houses bacteria that ferment the leaves, much as microbes in the stomachs of cattle ferment grass.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Though” belongs to the first clause: the hoatzin being well equipped for a diet of leaves contrasts with the previous sentence, which says leaves are poor food for most birds. The comma sets “though” off from that clause, and the semicolon joins it to the second independent clause, which explains what equips the bird for this diet.

A.recipe: semicolon with a non-clause (though as subordinator)
A.why_wrong: Placed after the semicolon, “though its enlarged crop houses bacteria ...” is a dependent clause, and a semicolon cannot join a main clause to a dependent clause.

B.why_wrong: A comma after “though” cannot join the two independent clauses “The hoatzin ... though” and “its enlarged crop houses bacteria ... grass.”

C.why_wrong: With no mark after it, “though” introduces a concession: the hoatzin is well equipped for leaves even though its crop houses bacteria that ferment them. But those bacteria are what equip it for the diet, so there is nothing to concede.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (avian digestion). Band 7: adverb closes clause 1 and answers the previous sentence; clause 2 gives the reason clause 1 is true (the crop’s bacteria), so the subordinate “though” reading in C has nothing to concede (CB 21e58a83, 5aa171de logic), and A fails by rule. Review: the earlier clause 2 (“it accomplishes this by fermenting”) let C read as a fair caveat.

fixes: second defensible option: C (“foliage, though it accomplishes this by fermenting the leaves”) read as a fair caveat, helped by sentence 1’s “without the help of symbiotic microbes”; clause 1 is now “is remarkably well equipped for such a diet” and clause 2 gives its reason (“its enlarged crop houses bacteria that ferment the leaves”), so the concession in C is illogical, as in CB 21e58a83 and 5aa171de; microbe phrase dropped from sentence 1; explanation, every why_wrong and notes rewritten
review.notes: No fact check (Boundaries, brief of 2026-10-16); named people are real and only their own known work is attributed to them; no invented names.

band7.why: Adverb closes clause 1 and answers the previous sentence; the taught “; though” pattern fails by rule and the subordinate “though” reading fails only on meaning (clause 2 is the reason clause 1 is true), the 5aa171de and 21e58a83 shape.

items.subtype: Supplementary “for one” closing clause 1, period before “Another”
items.passage: Numerous words in American English can be traced to the languages spoken by enslaved Africans. “Goober,” a regional term for the peanut, derives from the Kikongo word ______ example is “gumbo,” which comes from a Bantu term for okra, the vegetable traditionally used to thicken that dish.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “For one” marks “goober” as the first example of the words described in the previous sentence, so it belongs with that clause, set off by a comma. A period then separates that sentence from the next one, “Another example is ‘gumbo,’ ... that dish.”

A.why_wrong: Placing “For one” at the start of the second sentence labels “gumbo” as the first example, which contradicts “Another example.”

C.why_wrong: Commas around “for one” leave the two independent clauses joined by only a comma.

D.why_wrong: Nothing marks the end of the first clause before “for one,” and the comma after “for one” then splices two independent clauses.

items.notes: Subject: language (West African loanwords). Band 6: 5670a657 move (adverb closes clause 1, period after it) without its colon-list frame; the logic decoy A fails on the word “Another,” so it is wrong by construction.

review.notes: Kept: the “, for one. Another” move follows 5670a657, but it is the template’s listed for-one pattern (spec/rw/boundaries.md section 7) with a different frame and wording. “nguba” is left bare like other non-English words in the bank (CB prints them in italics; house style has no italics). No fact check (Boundaries, brief of 2026-10-16); named people are real and only their own known work is attributed to them; no invented names.

band7.why: “for one” closes clause 1 (5670a657, the template’s band-6 item; band 7 never uses “for one”); the logic decoy is killed by “Another,” in plain view right after the blank.

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a noun phrase with a relative clause
items.passage: Japanese poet Masaoka Shiki, who gave the haiku its modern name in the 1890s, believed the form had stagnated after centuries of conventional imitation. As a remedy, he urged writers to adopt a principle borrowed from Western-style ______ or “sketching from life,” an approach that required poets to record what they observed rather than recycle inherited imagery.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “As a remedy, he urged writers to adopt a principle borrowed from Western-style painting” is a complete clause, and what follows names that principle: “shasei, or ‘sketching from life,’ an approach that ...” A colon correctly introduces this explanation.

A.why_wrong: “Shasei ... an approach that required poets to record ...” has no main verb of its own (“required” belongs to “that”), so it cannot follow a semicolon.

C.why_wrong: Placing a period after “painting” makes “Shasei ... inherited imagery” a sentence fragment.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “painting shasei” runs the clause into the noun phrase that explains it.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Japanese poetry). Band 7: clause ends on an announcing noun (“a principle”) and the specified item is a noun phrase with its own appositive and a relative clause carrying the finite verb “required,” so the semicolon and period read as clause joints.

fixes: A and C why_wrong quoted wording the passage no longer has (“asked poets to describe”, “actually observed”); now quote “required poets to record” and “inherited imagery”
review.notes: No fact check (Boundaries, brief of 2026-10-16); named people are real and only their own known work is attributed to them; no invented names.

band7.why: Clause ends after an announcing noun (“a principle borrowed from Western-style painting”); the specified item is a term with a gloss and an appositive whose relative clause carries the finite verb “required” 11 words past the blank, so semicolon and period read as clause joints (f30a478e, e9aee0d8 shape).

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a two-part list
items.passage: Built between the fifteenth and twentieth centuries in China’s Fujian Province, the large earthen buildings known as tulou were designed to serve two functions at ______ for an extended family, sometimes hundreds of people in all, and protection from bandits, provided by fortified outer walls of rammed earth.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Built between ... the large earthen buildings known as tulou were designed to serve two functions at once” is a complete clause, and what follows names the two functions. A colon correctly introduces that list.

A.why_wrong: “Housing for an extended family ... and protection from bandits ...” is a list of noun phrases, not an independent clause, so a semicolon cannot join it to the first clause.

B.why_wrong: A period after “once” makes the list of the two functions a sentence fragment.

C.why_wrong: Without a colon, “at once housing” runs the clause into the list that explains it.

items.notes: Subject: arts (vernacular architecture). Band 6: one 48-word sentence; a long two-item list with internal commas and a participial tail follows the colon, so the period and semicolon versions look like sentence breaks (c468db1c move).

review.notes: No fact check (Boundaries, brief of 2026-10-16); named people are real and only their own known work is attributed to them; no invented names.

band7.why: Colon before a two-item list after “two functions at once” (c468db1c move); the announcing phrase sits at the blank, so the cue is local and nothing is decided by meaning.

items.subtype: Restrictive appositive (category noun plus title), then the verb
items.passage: Reflecting the importance of maize, which was domesticated in southern Mexico some 9,000 years ago and became the foundation of Mesoamerican diets, the K’iche’ Maya ______ describes the gods fashioning the first humans from maize dough after unsuccessful attempts to make them from mud and then wood.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Popol Vuh” is a restrictive appositive: it identifies which K’iche’ Maya text is meant, so no commas set it off. No punctuation belongs between the subject, “the K’iche’ Maya text Popol Vuh,” and its verb, “describes.”

B.why_wrong: Setting “Popol Vuh” off with commas treats the title as removable, but without it the sentence no longer says which text is meant.

C.why_wrong: A comma after “Popol Vuh” separates the subject from its verb, “describes.”

D.why_wrong: A single comma separates the descriptive noun phrase from the title it is identified by, and it has no partner.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Maya text). Band 7: non-person restrictive appositive with a category noun before the title (59a246dc move); nothing earlier singles out a text, so the comma pair is not defensible; the comma that ends the 22-word introductory phrase makes more commas look natural. Two slots vary across the options.

fixes: dropped “sixteenth-century” so the comma pair in B cannot be defended by reading “the sixteenth-century K’iche’ Maya text” as already naming a unique text; end now “after unsuccessful attempts to make them from mud and then wood” to keep the length check; explanation updated
review.notes: No fact check (Boundaries, brief of 2026-10-16); named people are real and only their own known work is attributed to them; no invented names.

band7.why: Non-person restrictive appositive with a category noun before a title (59a246dc, a band-7-only recipe), two slots varying across the options, and the 22-word introductory phrase ending in a comma makes the comma versions look natural.

items.subtype: Restrictive appositive (title plus name) in a compound subject
items.passage: Long presumed to have been constructed with a straightedge and compass, the girih patterns adorning many medieval Islamic buildings were reinterpreted in 2007, when ______ and his colleague Paul Steinhardt proposed that artisans assembled them from five decorated tile shapes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Peter Lu” is essential information identifying the physicist, so no punctuation separates the title from the name. No comma belongs after the name either, since “physicist Peter Lu and his colleague Paul Steinhardt” is a compound subject of “proposed.”

A.why_wrong: Commas around “Peter Lu” treat the name as removable, and the second comma also splits the compound subject before “and.”

B.why_wrong: A comma between the title “physicist” and the name it is identified by is not needed.

D.why_wrong: A comma before “and” in a two-part subject separates “physicist Peter Lu” from “his colleague Paul Steinhardt.”

items.notes: Subject: arts and mathematics (Islamic geometric design). Band 6: title plus name followed by a second subject (4dcedc31 move), inside a when-clause after an 11-word introductory participial phrase.

review.notes: No fact check (Boundaries, brief of 2026-10-16); named people are real and only their own known work is attributed to them; no invented names.

band7.why: Title plus name followed by “and his colleague” (4dcedc31 move); the rule is decided at the blank and the comma-around-name decoy is the standard one.

items.subtype: Opening a dash pair whose partner comes after an inner comma
items.passage: In the 1990s, divers off Japan’s Amami Islands began encountering mysterious geometric formations on the seafloor. The ______ nearly two meters in diameter, with ridges radiating symmetrically from the center like spokes of a wheel—proved to be the handiwork of male pufferfish courting females.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The dash after “wheel” closes a supplementary element describing the formations, so a dash must open it after “formations.” The pair of dashes sets “each nearly two meters in diameter ... wheel” apart from the subject, “The formations,” and its verb, “proved.”

A.why_wrong: The comma after “diameter” makes an opening comma look natural, but an element closed with a dash must also be opened with one.

B.why_wrong: With no mark after “formations,” the dash after “wheel” has no partner and splits the subject from its verb, “proved.”

D.why_wrong: “The formations” is not a complete clause, so a colon cannot follow it.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (fish courtship structures). Band 6 (no band-7 move intended): partner dash 18 words after the blank, with an inner comma that tempts the comma version.

review.notes: No fact check (Boundaries, brief of 2026-10-16); named people are real and only their own known work is attributed to them; no invented names.

band7.why: Dash pair with the partner 18 words past the blank and an inner comma tempting A, but one level of supplement only; band-7 dash items nest a second level (6e071432, 83898524).

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing appositive whose noun carries a relative clause
items.passage: Murujuga, on the coast of Western Australia, may contain more rock engravings than any other location. Among its estimated one million petroglyphs are depictions of the doglike marsupial known as the ______ detail that, because the animal vanished from mainland Australia roughly 3,000 years ago, helps archaeologists date some of the engravings.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause ends with “known as the thylacine.” The noun phrase “a detail that, because the animal vanished ..., helps archaeologists date some of the engravings” is a nonessential element commenting on that whole clause, and a comma correctly separates it from the clause.

B.why_wrong: The verb “helps” belongs to the relative clause beginning with “that,” so “a detail that ... helps archaeologists date some of the engravings” is not an independent clause and cannot follow a semicolon.

C.why_wrong: A period after “thylacine” makes “A detail that ... helps archaeologists date some of the engravings” a sentence fragment.

D.why_wrong: With no comma, “thylacine a detail” runs the noun phrase into the clause it comments on.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (Aboriginal rock art). Band 7: sentence appositive (“a detail that, because ..., helps”) whose relative clause has an interrupting because-clause before its finite verb, so the period and semicolon versions read like “A detail ... helps archaeologists date ...” (0b005ae2, e67f9967 shape); 37-word inverted main clause. Review: was a plain appositive on “thylacine,” which reads band 6.

fixes: the trailing element was a plain appositive renaming “thylacine” (“a striped marsupial predator that ...”), which reads band 6; now a sentence appositive with an interrupted relative clause (“a detail that, because the animal vanished ..., helps archaeologists date some of the engravings”), the 0b005ae2 and e67f9967 shape; explanation, every why_wrong and notes rewritten
review.notes: No fact check (Boundaries, brief of 2026-10-16); named people are real and only their own known work is attributed to them; no invented names.

band7.why: Sentence appositive whose relative clause puts a because-clause before its finite verb, so “A detail ... helps archaeologists date ...” looks like a sentence after a period or semicolon; the cue (no main verb outside “that”) is 15 or more words past the blank in a 37-word inverted run.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a long subject ending in a name and its verb
items.passage: The meticulous diary kept from 1785 to 1812 by Maine midwife Martha ______ documents more than 800 deliveries along with the economic and social life of her frontier community.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The meticulous diary kept from 1785 to 1812 by Maine midwife Martha Ballard” is the subject of the sentence, and “documents” is its verb. No punctuation belongs between a subject and its verb.

A.why_wrong: The long subject makes a pause feel natural, but a comma cannot separate the subject from its verb, “documents.”

B.why_wrong: A colon cannot come between a subject and its verb.

C.why_wrong: A single dash between the subject and its verb has no role in the sentence.

items.notes: Subject: history (early American social history). Band 6 by rule (no band-7 subject-verb items): 13-word subject ending in a title-plus-name, so a comma after the name feels natural (f868d438 move).

fixes: explanation quoted “The diary kept” for the passage’s “The meticulous diary kept”
review.notes: No fact check (Boundaries, brief of 2026-10-16); named people are real and only their own known work is attributed to them; no invented names.

band7.why: S4_subj_verb has no band-7 official items; a strong band 6 (13-word subject ending in a title plus name, f868d438 move).

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses with a comma and and
items.passage: Leaf-cutting ants of the species Acromyrmex echinatior grow underground fungus gardens, which they feed with fragments of leaves. In 2020, researchers found the ants’ bodies coated in a thin layer of magnesium-rich ______ in staged fights with larger ants, this mineral armor helped the coated ants survive.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In 2020, researchers ... magnesium-rich calcite” and “in staged fights with larger ants, this mineral armor helped the coated ants survive” are both independent clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “and” correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: The two independent clauses run together with no punctuation or conjunction.

C.why_wrong: When “and” joins two long independent clauses like these, a comma is needed before it.

D.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses, even when the second begins with an introductory phrase.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (insect biomineralization). The second clause opens with a 6-word introductory phrase, as in 2.2 and 2.5. Review: clause 1 was “discovered that ...,” so C could read as a second, comma-free complement of “discovered”; now a plain main clause.

fixes: C was defensible: with clause 1 “researchers discovered that the ants’ bodies are coated ...,” “and in staged fights ... this mineral armor helped” could read as a second complement of “discovered,” which needs no comma; clause 1 is now “researchers found the ants’ bodies coated in ...,” so the “and” clause can only be a second main clause
review.notes: No fact check (Boundaries, brief of 2026-10-16); named people are real and only their own known work is attributed to them; no invented names.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a short introductory phrase
items.passage: Nan Madol, a complex of nearly 100 artificial islets off the coast of Pohnpei in Micronesia, was constructed from huge columns of basalt, some weighing several tons. It was the political center of the Saudeleur dynasty until about ______ this day, archaeologists debate how the builders transported the columns from their quarries.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “It was the political center of the Saudeleur dynasty until about 1628” is a complete sentence, and “To this day, archaeologists debate ...” is another. A period correctly separates them.

A.why_wrong: A comma cannot join the two independent clauses, even though the second begins with “to this day.”

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “until about 1628 to this day” runs the two sentences together.

C.why_wrong: “And” without a comma does not properly join two long independent clauses, and it attaches “to this day” to the first one.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (Micronesia). 3-word opener (“To this day,”) after the period, as in 2.7 and 2.27.

review.notes: No fact check (Boundaries, brief of 2026-10-16); named people are real and only their own known work is attributed to them; no invented names.

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing participial phrase
items.passage: In about 1615, Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala, an Indigenous Andean nobleman, completed a nearly 1,200-page manuscript addressed to King Philip III of Spain and filled it with almost 400 pen-and-ink ______ the abuses that colonial officials and priests inflicted on Andean communities.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In about 1615, Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala ... filled it with almost 400 pen-and-ink drawings” is a main clause, and “documenting the abuses ...” is a participial phrase that adds information about it. A comma correctly separates the two.

B.why_wrong: “Documenting the abuses ...” has no subject or main verb, so it cannot follow a semicolon.

C.why_wrong: A period makes “Documenting the abuses ... communities” a sentence fragment.

D.why_wrong: “And” would need to join two parts of the same kind, but nothing before it matches the phrase “documenting the abuses ...”; the sentence breaks.

items.notes: Subject: history (colonial Andean chronicle).

review.notes: No fact check (Boundaries, brief of 2026-10-16); named people are real and only their own known work is attributed to them; no invented names.

items.subtype: Opening a comma pair around an appositive
items.passage: The box jellyfish Tripedalia ______ a fingernail-sized species living in Caribbean mangrove swamps, has 24 eyes, four of which always point upward, allowing the jellyfish to see the mangrove canopy through the water’s surface and remain near the roots, where its prey gathers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The comma after “swamps” closes a nonessential appositive describing the jellyfish, so a comma must open it after “cystophora.” The pair of commas sets “a fingernail-sized species ... swamps” apart from the subject and its verb, “has.”

A.why_wrong: Without a comma after “cystophora,” the comma after “swamps” has no partner and splits the subject from its verb, “has.”

B.why_wrong: A dash cannot open an element that is closed with a comma.

D.why_wrong: “The box jellyfish Tripedalia cystophora” is not a complete clause, so a colon cannot follow it.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (animal vision). Partner comma 8 words after the blank.

items.subtype: Closing a dash pair before the verb
items.passage: Among the Sámi people of northern Scandinavia, a joik—a traditional chant through which a singer evokes a particular person, animal, or landscape rather than describing ______ is often intensely personal: in childhood, many Sámi receive a joik that belongs to them alone.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The dash after “joik” opens a supplementary element that defines the term, so a dash must close it after “describing it.” The pair of dashes separates “a traditional chant ... describing it” from the subject, “a joik,” and its verb, “is.”

A.why_wrong: The commas in the list “person, animal, or landscape” make a comma look natural, but an element opened with a dash must be closed with a dash.

C.why_wrong: A semicolon cannot close a dash element, and it would split the subject from its verb, “is.”

D.why_wrong: Without a closing dash, the element opened after “joik” runs straight into the verb “is.”

items.notes: Subject: arts (Indigenous vocal music). Partner dash 17 words before the blank, with list commas inside the element.

fixes: “receive a joik in childhood that belongs to them alone” let the that-clause attach to “childhood”; now “in childhood, many Sámi receive a joik that belongs to them alone”; explanation and A why_wrong quoted wording the passage does not have (“a chant”, “person, animal, or place”)
review.notes: No fact check (Boundaries, brief of 2026-10-16); named people are real and only their own known work is attributed to them; no invented names.

items.subtype: Semicolon before a conjunctive adverb that opens clause 2
items.passage: For decades, most public libraries in the United States charged fines for overdue books. Librarians generally assumed that the fines encouraged borrowers to return items on ______ after Chicago’s public library system eliminated late fines in 2019, the number of long-overdue items that borrowers brought back rose sharply within a few weeks.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The semicolon joins two independent clauses, and “however” begins the second one. It signals the contrast between librarians’ assumption that fines encouraged returns and what happened in Chicago when fines were dropped.

B.why_wrong: Placing “however” at the end of the first clause signals that the librarians’ assumption contrasts with the previous sentence, but it simply explains why libraries charged fines.

C.why_wrong: Nothing marks the boundary between the two independent clauses before “however.”

D.why_wrong: Commas around “however” cannot join two independent clauses.

items.notes: Subject: social science (public policy). Clause 1 agrees with the first sentence, so B’s contrast fails by construction.

review.notes: No fact check (Boundaries, brief of 2026-10-16); named people are real and only their own known work is attributed to them; no invented names.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: Tingatinga, a painting style that emerged in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, in the late 1960s, is named after its founder, Edward Saidi Tingatinga. The style is celebrated ______ its bold outlines, vivid enamel colors, and whimsical depictions of animals.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The preposition “for” is followed by its objects, “its bold outlines, vivid enamel colors, and whimsical depictions of animals.” No punctuation belongs between a preposition and its object.

A.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, and “The style is celebrated for” is not one.

B.why_wrong: A comma cannot separate the preposition “for” from its objects.

C.why_wrong: A dash cannot separate the preposition “for” from its objects.

items.notes: Subject: arts (East African painting).

fixes: explanation and A why_wrong quoted an older wording (“known for”, “bright enamel colors, and playful images”); now match the passage

items.subtype: No punctuation between a verb and its object
items.passage: Many animals appear to experience REM sleep, a stage characterized by rapid eye movements. Jumping spiders cannot move their eyes, but they can shift their retinas. Because juvenile spiders have translucent bodies, researchers in Germany could ______ these retinas twitching as the animals slept suspended from silk threads at night.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “These retinas twitching ...” is the object of the verb “observe.” No punctuation belongs between a verb and its object.

A.why_wrong: A colon cannot come between a verb and its object.

C.why_wrong: A comma cannot separate the verb “observe” from its object.

D.why_wrong: A dash cannot separate the verb “observe” from its object.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (animal sleep).

items.subtype: Embedded question: statement word order and a period
items.passage: A face may look more attractive in a group photo than in a photo by itself. In 2014, two psychologists investigated whether ______ They found that people rated the same faces as more attractive when they appeared in a group.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: is this so-called cheerleader effect real?
this so-called cheerleader effect is real?
this so-called cheerleader effect is real.
is this so-called cheerleader effect real.
items.explanation: “Whether this so-called cheerleader effect is real” is an embedded question, part of a statement about what the psychologists tested. It takes statement word order (subject before verb), and the sentence ends with a period.

A.why_wrong: Inverted word order and a question mark belong to a direct question, but this one is embedded in a statement.

B.recipe: question errors (question mark on a statement)
B.why_wrong: The word order is right, but the sentence is a statement, so it ends with a period.

D.why_wrong: An embedded question keeps statement word order, so “is” should follow “this so-called cheerleader effect.”

items.notes: Subject: social science (perception of faces).

review.notes: No fact check (Boundaries, brief of 2026-10-16); named people are real and only their own known work is attributed to them; no invented names.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses with a comma and and
items.passage: Eucalyptus trees in Western Australia can send their roots dozens of meters underground to reach ______ trees growing above buried gold deposits sometimes carry tiny particles of gold in their leaves.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Eucalyptus trees ... to reach water” and “trees growing above buried gold deposits sometimes carry tiny particles of gold in their leaves” are both independent clauses. A comma followed by “and” correctly joins them.

B.why_wrong: When “and” joins two long independent clauses like these, a comma is needed before it.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

D.why_wrong: The two independent clauses run together with no punctuation or conjunction.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (botany and geology).

review.notes: No fact check (Boundaries, brief of 2026-10-16); named people are real and only their own known work is attributed to them; no invented names.

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory dependent clause
items.passage: Sandgrouse frequently nest in deserts many kilometers from the nearest water. When a male sandgrouse visits a watering hole during the breeding ______ he saturates his specialized belly feathers, which absorb water like a sponge, and transports it back to his thirsty chicks.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “When a male sandgrouse visits a watering hole during the breeding season” is a dependent clause that introduces the main clause, “he saturates his specialized belly feathers ....” A comma correctly separates the two.

A.why_wrong: Without a comma, nothing marks where the introductory clause ends and the main clause begins.

B.why_wrong: The “When” clause is dependent, so a semicolon cannot join it to the main clause.

C.why_wrong: A period makes “When a male sandgrouse ... season” a sentence fragment.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (bird parenting).

fixes: explanation quoted “a water source” for the passage’s “a watering hole”
review.notes: No fact check (Boundaries, brief of 2026-10-16); named people are real and only their own known work is attributed to them; no invented names.

items.subtype: Commas between items in a simple series
items.passage: As early as 400 BCE, communities in the deserts of Persia preserved ice through the summer in yakhchāls, tall domed structures built over deep underground pits. Their thick walls were made of sarooj, a heat-resistant mortar composed of sand, ______ egg whites, lime, goat hair, and ash.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Sand, clay, egg whites, lime, goat hair, and ash” is a list of the mortar’s ingredients. A comma correctly separates “clay” from the next item, as the other items in the list are separated.

A.why_wrong: Without a comma, “clay egg whites” runs two items of the list together.

C.why_wrong: Semicolons separate list items only when the items contain commas themselves; these simple items are separated by commas.

D.why_wrong: A colon cannot be used in the middle of a list to separate one item from the next.

items.notes: Subject: history (Persian architecture).

review.notes: No fact check (Boundaries, brief of 2026-10-16); named people are real and only their own known work is attributed to them; no invented names.

items.subtype: No punctuation before a restrictive that clause
items.passage: In the 1980s, Indian architect Balkrishna Doshi designed Aranya, a low-cost housing project in the city of Indore. Rather than finished houses, the project gave thousands of families modest ______ that came with water and sewer connections. Residents could then build and gradually enlarge their homes as their household incomes increased.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause beginning with “that” is restrictive: it tells which plots the families received and is essential to the sentence. No punctuation belongs between “plots” and the restrictive clause that follows it.

A.why_wrong: A comma cannot separate “plots” from the restrictive clause beginning with “that.”

B.why_wrong: A dash cannot separate “plots” from the restrictive clause beginning with “that.”

D.why_wrong: “And” would need to join two parts of the same kind, but “that came with water and sewer connections” describes the plots; it is not a second item.

items.notes: Subject: social science (urban housing policy). Review: rewritten; “In the 1980s, architect X designed Y, a low-cost housing project that gave thousands of families ...” with the same four options (comma, dash, no mark, comma plus “and”) copied official 1.17 (603755a5).
